extracted.intended_audience: aspiring fiction writers and authors seeking agents/publishers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for fiction writers on craft (characters, plot, POV, etc.), submitting to agents/editors, navigating contracts and publicity, self-publishing, competitions, and joining the writing community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agent selection and relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: When agents request further contact or meetings, assess whether there is a 'shared vision' and whether the agent feels right for you; your relationship with your agent will be a crucial one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple agents express interest, arrange conversations or meetings promptly to determine fit. Make a decision swiftly when offered representation (likened to a proposal of marriage) and inform others politely, sending thank-you notes to those you decline. If only one agent is interested but it doesn't feel right after meeting, do not sign—contact others. The relationship with an agent is long-term; choose someone whose vision matches yours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware nonlegitimate agents
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid agents who solicit manuscripts via advertisements or request reading fees; bona fide agents do not need to place ads and do not charge authors to read manuscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Red flags: 'invitation to submit' ads, requests for money (reading fees), referral to 'editors' who charge authors with agent kickbacks. Legitimate agents make money from sales, not author fees, and do not charge for reading or signing clients. Verify membership in professional bodies (e.g., Association of Authors' Representatives/AAR), ask for a list of recent sales, and investigate an agent's track record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of responses to submissions and how to interpret them
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions typically elicit no response, a form rejection, a personalized rejection, a rejection with invitation to resubmit, or an acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No response: let it go (busy/jaded readers). Form rejection: common; not necessarily a judgment of poor work. Personalized rejection: rare and may indicate promise. Rejection with invitation to resubmit: encouraging—incorporate suggestions into a rewrite and resubmit with a copy of their letter and a thank-you. Acceptance: celebrate. Keep perspective—rejection is common; continue writing and submitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission record-keeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep track of what you send to whom and when, including reasons for rejection or acceptance patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A submission log prevents sending the same person multiple submissions, helps you follow up when appropriate, and can reveal patterns (e.g., success with particular magazines). Recording acceptances is useful for morale and market insight. Treat writing as a small business—develop good administrative and record-keeping habits to maximize writing time and reduce stress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectations about money, advances, and royalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Earnings vary widely; typical novel advances are often between about $5,000 and $25,000, royalties commonly range from 7 to 15 percent of cover price and may be stepped for higher sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An advance is essentially a loan paid against future royalties; authors 'pay back' advances through royalties. New writers seldom get large advances. Consider the market value publishers assign, and recognize luck plays a role. Publishing can create secondary opportunities (speaking, teaching, commissions); be entrepreneurial about creating income streams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contracts: scrutiny and protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing contracts govern the use and sale of your work and can be complex, especially regarding electronic rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have contracts examined by your agent and, if desired, an entertainment or literary property lawyer. Consult professional organizations (e.g., National Writers Union, Authors Guild) for contract advice. Learn contract basics yourself—read clause by clause, obtain guides to contract law for writers, and never feel pressured to sign a contract you are uncomfortable with.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working with editor and prepublication process
rubrics_metrics.description: After a book deal, you'll work with an editor to revise and improve your manuscript; revisions may be extensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect oral or written editorial notes and be prepared for more than minor tinkering. Your editor also acts as an in-house ally advocating for your book with sales, marketing, and publicity. Understand that publishers have lists and priorities; cultivate the editor relationship to secure attention for your book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicity and self-promotion (author responsibilities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicists will promote your book, but you should also prepare to do your own promotion and make it easy for booksellers and media to work with you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare a media kit (press release, author photo, bio sheet, contact details, prepublication endorsements, and a copy of the book or jacket). Call booksellers to arrange signings/workshops and be cooperative. Establish an author website from day one (domain name, photo, bio, personal spin); if necessary, hire a professional to design it. Be proactive in marketing; publicists may prioritize more profitable authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-publishing and vanity publishers
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-publishing via print-on-demand and publishing services is accessible and affordable but these services are not selective; vanity/subsidy publishers charge fees and may produce shoddy work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If self-publishing, hire a good freelance editor to ensure quality control. Distinguish legitimate publishing services (which provide production services) from vanity publishers (which pretend to be publishers and solicit payment). Be aware that self-published books rarely turn a profit and that vanity publishers will often overcharge and deliver poor results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entering competitions, grants, and awards
rubrics_metrics.description: Competitions and grants can provide prestige, money, publication, or agent exposure, but some charge entry fees and legitimacy varies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research competitions and sponsoring organizations (market guides, magazines, internet searches). Verify legitimacy—many charge entry fees, but check the sponsor's reputation. Awards can lead to publication and agent interest; even semifinalist status can enhance query letters. Grants and fellowships (e.g., NEA, state arts councils) may require credits or nominations but are worth pursuing for financial support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engaging with the writing community
rubrics_metrics.description: Join conferences, retreats, readings, classes, writing groups, and professional organizations to sustain motivation, learn, network, and gain industry access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conferences: opportunities to meet publishing professionals, attend seminars, and network; agents often speak. Retreats/writers' colonies: provide focused time to write with minimal distractions; some are selective and provide funding. Literary readings and local events offer community contact. Writing classes provide expert instruction and feedback; writing groups offer peer critique and support. Consider joining professional organizations (National Writers Union, Authors Guild, PEN) for networking, contract advice, advocacy, and other services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daily discipline and prioritizing writing
rubrics_metrics.description: To become and be a writer, set aside regular writing time, treat it as sacrosanct, and make craft and submission activities habitual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust to daily discipline (writing several days a week or daily). Use rituals (e.g., preparing tea) to transition into writing. If you can't quit your day job immediately, reconcile it with writing by scheduling and protecting writing time. Having several projects on the go helps weather rejection. The best way to become a writer is to get serious about practicing regularly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing external interruptions and setting boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipate family/friend intrusions and set firm boundaries so your writing time is protected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain to loved ones that writing is important, bolt the door, and learn to say no to requests that undermine writing time. While there will be occasions to prioritize others, protect your writing time to avoid chronic sabotage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing creative blocks and emotional setbacks (the 'Abyss')
rubrics_metrics.description: Creative despair ('the Abyss') can strike suddenly and undermine confidence; use social contact and healthy lifestyle practices as antidotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stay connected with real people and the writing community to combat isolation. Maintain a healthful lifestyle—proper diet, sleep, fresh air, and physical activity—to support mood and productivity. When blocked, write anyway: freewrite, brainstorm, and work on other projects. Use exercise and social contact to energize body and mind and help words flow again.

rubrics_metrics.name: CHARACTER (cheat sheet)
rubrics_metrics.description: Checklist items to evaluate characters: desires, distinctiveness, contrasting traits, consistency, capacity for change, depth of knowledge about them, round vs flat appropriateness, showing vs telling, use of showing methods, and names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do your characters have desires? Are your characters distinctive enough not to be types? Do your characters have contrasting traits that make them complex? Are your characters consistent despite their contrasting traits? Do your characters have the ability to change? Do you know your characters well enough? Are the right characters 'round' and the right characters 'flat'? Are you showing your characters more than telling about them? Are you utilizing all four methods of showing—action, speech, appearance, thought? Do your characters have the right names?

rubrics_metrics.name: PLOT (cheat sheet)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot checklist: presence of a major dramatic question, protagonist with strong goal and obstacles (external and internal), clear beginning/middle/end, appropriate exposition in opening, escalating conflict, cause-and-effect linking in middle, crisis/climax/consequences at end, and plausible satisfying ending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do you have a major dramatic question? Do you have a protagonist with a strong goal and plenty of obstacles? Does your protagonist have both external and internal obstacles? Do you have a beginning, middle, and end? Is your beginning not clogged with too much exposition and not too long? Does your conflict escalate in the middle? Are the events of your middle linked by cause and effect? Do you have crisis, climax, and consequences at the end? Is your ending plausible, satisfying, and not too long?

rubrics_metrics.name: POINT OF VIEW (cheat sheet)
rubrics_metrics.description: POV checklist: choose first/second/third person, single-vision vs multiple-vision, consider omniscient or objective POV, emotional closeness of narrator in second/third person, and consistency of POV.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Does your story work best in first, second, or third person? Does your story work best with a single-vision or multiple-vision POV? Is there any reason your story might work best with the omniscient or objective POV? If you're using a second- or third-person narrator, how close emotionally is the narrator to the story and characters? Are you keeping your POV consistent?

rubrics_metrics.name: DESCRIPTION (cheat sheet)
rubrics_metrics.description: Description checklist: use all five senses, be specific, avoid overusing adjectives/adverbs, use figurative/lyrical techniques where appropriate, avoid overdone description that chokes the story, use telling details, avoid clichés and mixed metaphors, and ensure descriptions reflect the POV character's consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Are your descriptions utilizing all five senses? Are your descriptions specific enough? Are you overusing adjectives and adverbs? Are you using figurative language and lyrical techniques where appropriate? Are your descriptions overdone, choking your story? Are you using telling details? Are you watching out for such description traps as clichés and mixed metaphors? Do your descriptions reflect the consciousness of your POV character or characters?

rubrics_metrics.name: DIALOGUE (cheat sheet)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue checklist: use dialogue and scenes for important points, make dialogue sound real but economical, avoid tags that draw attention, use stage directions to enhance dialogue, give characters distinctive voices appropriate to them, use subtext, and avoid clunky exposition or off-putting dialect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Are you using dialogue and scenes for the more important points in your story? Does your dialogue sound real yet also get to the point quickly? Do your tags call too much attention to themselves? Are you using stage directions to enhance your dialogue? Do your characters sound distinctive from one another and appropriate to who they are? Is there anywhere your dialogue can be improved by using subtext? Does your dialogue contain clunky exposition or off-putting dialect?

rubrics_metrics.name: SETTING / PACING (cheat sheet)
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting and pacing checklist: ground the story in specific place/time, let place/time affect action, use setting to enhance atmosphere/mood, have characters react to settings, avoid description that slows action, and choose places to expand/compress time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have you grounded your story in a specific place, or places? Have you grounded your story in a specific time, or times? Do the place and time of your story affect the action? Are there opportunities to let the setting enhance the atmosphere or mood? Do your characters act in a way that reflects either their comfort or discomfort with their setting? Are you describing your settings so much that they slow down the action? Have you chosen the right places either to expand or to compress time?

rubrics_metrics.name: VOICE (cheat sheet)
rubrics_metrics.description: Voice checklist: pick a voice that harmonizes with POV, narrator personality, and emotional distance; support voice with word/sentence/paragraph choices; keep voice consistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have you picked a voice that works in harmony with your POV choice, the personality of your narrator, and the narrator's emotional distance to the story? Do your word, sentence, and paragraph choices support your voice? Does your voice remain consistent throughout the story?

rubrics_metrics.name: THEME (cheat sheet)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theme checklist: identify a theme and handle it with a light touch; ensure all story elements support the theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have you identified a theme for your story? Does your theme surround your story with a light enough touch? Do all the elements of your story work to support the theme?

rubrics_metrics.name: REVISION (cheat sheet)
rubrics_metrics.description: Revision checklist: gain distance, consider reenvisioning, examine Big Things and Little Things, cut and tweak extensively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have you gotten enough distance from your story to begin the revision process? Have you considered reenvisioning your story? Have you looked through a magnifying glass at all the Big Things in your story? Have you looked through a microscope at all the Little Things in your story? Have you cut and tweaked as much as you possibly can?
